sections.html:
Nashua sits in southern New Hampshire, in southeastern Hillsborough County, and shares the county seat role with Manchester. Population is 92,435, and the city covers 31.73 square miles, of which 30.83 are land. The Massachusetts line is close, which shapes who shops and who buys here. Because New Hampshire has no sales tax, South Nashua's shopping district, anchored by Pheasant Lane Mall, pulls in shoppers from Massachusetts.

The city grew from textile mills into financial and professional services, high technology and defense. BAE Systems, Dell and Oracle have operations here, and two medical centers, Southern New Hampshire Medical Center and St. Joseph Hospital, serve the area.

Nashua is usually described by district, and each has a different housing feel. These come up most when owners describe where a house sits:

  • Downtown, centered on Main Street, the oldest commercial district
  • The Tree Streets, a neighborhood near downtown reached by the Broad Street Parkway
  • The Millyard, the former mill district and the Nashua Manufacturing Company Historic District
  • French Hill, the northern area once called Nashville
  • The Amherst Street corridor (NH 101A) in the northwest
  • South Nashua, near the Massachusetts line

Living in or next to a historic district? Find out from the city what review exterior work needs before you count it as a pre-sale repair.

Nashua's 2025 tax rate is $16.83 per $1,000 of valuation, up 93 cents, or 5.83 percent, from the year before.

Tax years run from April 1 to March 31. July 1 is the due date for the first bill, which uses half of last year's rate as an estimate. Once the state sets the new rate, the second bill follows, generally due by December 20. Abatement requests close March 1.

Nashua prorates property taxes by the day from April 1 when a home is bought or sold. The closing agent calculates your portion for the settlement statement.

If you sold the property but still receive a bill, forward it to the current owner, or return it in the envelope with a note giving the sale date and the buyer's name. A new owner may see the old name for a while, since the Registry of Deeds has to send the transfer to the Assessor's Office. The city's property tax self-service portal shows what is owed, which makes it easy to confirm a zero balance before you pick a closing date.

sections.h2: How to challenge a Nashua assessment
sections.html:
Ask the Assessor's Office, at 603-589-3040, to review the data, then file a written abatement application by March 1. A request that misses March 1 cannot be acted on for the current tax year. You may still ask for a spring review, in which the Assessing Department may look at your value for the following tax year.

State law covers the next steps. The city answers by July 1, and if you want to go further, pick the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or superior court, never both, and file by September 1. The abatement does not stop collection, so pay the bill. A homeowner planning to sell should decide early whether the effort is worth it, since a buyer will care more about future bills than a past refund.

RSA 78-B gives New Hampshire a transfer tax of $.75 per $100 of the price, and the buyer and seller each owe it. Granite Tax Connect takes the filing.

Selling a one to four family home means a written statement under RSA 477:4-d covering private water and sewage systems, insulation, any federally designated flood hazard zone and any underground heating oil tank. Ask the title company what other charges will appear at closing, such as a mortgage payoff or any unpaid tax.

sections.h2: Winter, water and the buyer's inspection
sections.html:
Nashua has cold winters and wet springs, so a buyer's inspector will usually look at:

  • Roof condition after snow and ice
  • Basement moisture and lot drainage
  • Heating equipment and fuel storage
  • Insulation, which the state disclosure form asks about

Fixing small items before listing can help a financed sale hold together. Skipping that work is possible: a buyer paying cash as-is takes most of the list off the table.

The Everett Turnpike is the main highway, and U.S. 3 follows it from the Massachusetts border to Exit 7E. NH 101A (Amherst Street), NH 111 (Hollis Street), NH 111A and NH 130 (Broad Street) also serve the city. The Broad Street Parkway, completed in 2015, connects Exit 6 to downtown.

The Nashua Transit System operates nine bus routes, and Boston Express runs from the Nashua Transit Center, near Exit 8, to South Station and Logan Airport. Nashua Airport (Boire Field) handles general aviation only, so air travelers use Manchester-Boston Regional or Logan. Commuter rail to Boston is only a proposal, so do not count on it when you price a house.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works in Nashua
sections.html:
Selling for cash in Nashua works like this: describe the house, review the offer and accept or pass, with no repairs and no lender appraisal. Title search, tax proration and the state transfer tax still happen. Ask the buyer to put the closing date, the price and who pays each closing cost in writing, and read the offer slowly before you sign. A fair buyer will not rush you, and you can say no at any point before closing.

Plan on three things before closing: a current tax payoff or confirmation that nothing is owed, your mortgage payoff if you have one, and a decision about what stays in the house. Once those are settled, the closing date is yours to pick within the title company's schedule.

sections.h2: Paperwork to gather before you list
sections.html:
Before you talk to a buyer or an agent, collect your latest tax bill, a copy of your deed and any permits for finished spaces or additions. Look up your account on the city portal to confirm nothing is owed, and call the Assessor's Office if the property record shows a different size or condition than the house really has. If you plan to ask for a spring review, note the date so it does not slip past March 1.

Add a short list of known repairs, including the roof, the heating system and any damp spots in the basement. Buyers and inspectors will find them anyway, and a seller who names them first usually keeps more control of the price. Photos taken before the house is emptied can also help if a question comes up later about what condition it was in.

faqs.q: What is the Nashua tax rate for 2025?
faqs.a: It is $16.83 per $1,000 of valuation, up from $15.90 in 2024.

faqs.q: When are Nashua property tax bills due?
faqs.a: July 1 is the first due date, on a bill estimated at half of last year's rate. The second bill comes after the state sets the rate and is generally due by December 20.

faqs.q: Are Nashua property taxes prorated when I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. The city prorates by the day starting April 1 when a home changes hands, and the closing agent shows your share.

faqs.q: What if I missed the March 1 abatement deadline in Nashua?
faqs.a: No action can be taken for that tax year. You may request a spring review, which may lead to a review of your value for the following year.

faqs.q: Is there a sales tax or transfer tax on a Nashua house sale?
faqs.a: Buyer and seller each owe a state transfer tax of $.75 per $100 of the price. New Hampshire has no general sales tax.
